meta.title: About Joe Apolenar — The Strongest
meta.description: Joe Apolenar: natural IPF powerlifter (−120 kg), former 155 kg athlete turned 115 kg competitor, retail operations manager, and full-stack builder of The Strongest.

hero.lead: The Strongest is not just a fitness brand. It is the intersection of elite strength and professional management systems — built by a natural IPF powerlifter who also ran retail operations and ships full-stack platforms.

transformation.title: 155 kg → 115 kg
transformation.subtitle: 342 lbs → 253 lbs · Two years
transformation.body1: A grueling two-year body transformation. Not a challenge. Not a hype cycle. Relentless discipline and consistency — session after session, decision after decision — until the scale and the platform both moved.
transformation.body2: That process is the same operating system behind every programme here: structure under pressure, measurable progress, and zero tolerance for random effort.

numbers.title: The Numbers
numbers.lead: Natural IPF powerlifter in the −120 kg class. Best lifts below — competition and gym standards, not marketing fiction.

mindset.corporate_body: Extensive background as Store and Area Manager for massive retail chains — Amazon, Tesco, Kaufland, Lidl — plus a degree in Managerial Psychology and IT. Leading people, processes, and results under real operational pressure.
mindset.fullstack_body: Full-stack developer building custom platforms with Next.js, Tailwind, and Supabase — the same stack powering The Strongest.
mindset.pullquote: Managing massive retail operations and coding full-stack apps requires the exact same structured, systematic approach as peaking for a 310 kg deadlift. That is why the training programmes here are systems — not random workouts.

philosophy.body: The Will of Fire is the bridge: elite physical strength and professional management systems, forced into one operating standard. Show up. Execute the plan. Measure what matters. Repeat until the result is inevitable.

strength.linear: Primary goal is general strength — linear progression is a clear fit.
strength.dup: DUP still supports strength with weekly variation.
strength.hybrid: Powerbuilding keeps strength primary with accessory volume.

powerlifting.dup: Powerlifting goal favors undulating SBD emphasis.
powerlifting.conjugate: Conjugate is a powerlifting-oriented advanced option.
powerlifting.block: Block sequencing suits structured powerlifting prep.

hypertrophy.hybrid: Hypertrophy priority maps to the powerbuilding hybrid.
hypertrophy.dup: DUP includes hypertrophy-oriented days in the week.
hypertrophy.linear: Linear still builds base strength that supports muscle work.

comp.block: Competition prep favors sequenced accumulation → realization.
comp.dup: DUP can peak toward a meet with rising specificity.
comp.conjugate: Conjugate can increase specificity late in a cycle.

beginner.linear: Beginner experience scores highest on simple linear structure.
beginner.hybrid: Hybrid is usable later; linear is safer first.
beginner.highFreq: High frequency is penalized until technique and recovery are proven.
beginner.block: True block concentration is usually unnecessary for beginners.

intermediate.dup: Intermediate lifters often respond well to weekly undulation.
intermediate.hybrid: Intermediates can handle strength + hypertrophy dual focus.
intermediate.block: Blocks become useful once progress is no longer automatic.
intermediate.linear: Linear remains viable if you prefer simplicity.

advanced.conjugate: Advanced lifters can tolerate ME/DE rotation.
advanced.highFreq: Advanced recovery literacy supports higher frequency.
advanced.block: Concentrated blocks suit advanced preparation windows.
advanced.dup: DUP remains a strong advanced powerlifting option.
advanced.linear: Long exclusive linear phases score lower for advanced lifters.

3.linear: 3 training days fit a focused linear template.
3.dup: DUP has a clear 3-day SBD split.
3.highFreq: High-frequency SBD needs more than 3 days to make sense.
3.conjugate: Classic conjugate structure expects a 4-day week.

4.dup: 4 days is a strong DUP schedule.
4.highFreq: 4 days can start a moderated high-frequency plan.

5.conjugate: Extra day can hold special-exercise work.

6.highFreq: 6 days is the clearest match for high-frequency SBD.
6.hybrid: 6 days can work if recovery is managed.
6.linear: 6 days usually exceeds what a simple linear plan needs.

weak.dup: Weak {lift} can get extra emphasis inside undulating days.
weak.highFreq: Weak {lift} benefits from more frequent practice exposures.
weak.none: No single weak lift — balanced linear work is fine.

poor.linear: Poor recovery favors lower complexity and clearer fatigue control.
poor.dup: DUP can stay moderate if RPE is capped.
poor.highFreq: High frequency is heavily penalized when recovery is poor.
poor.conjugate: Conjugate max-effort stress is a poor match for low recovery.
poor.block: Accumulation blocks are risky when recovery is already poor.
poor.hybrid: Hybrid accessory volume adds fatigue when recovery is limited.

okay.dup: Okay recovery supports moderate undulating stress.
okay.linear: Okay recovery pairs well with simple progressive overload.
okay.hybrid: Hybrid is usable with careful accessory dosing.
okay.block: Blocks are possible if accumulation stays honest.
okay.highFreq: High frequency remains a cautious choice on okay recovery.

good.highFreq: Good recovery unlocks higher training frequency.
good.conjugate: Good recovery supports max-effort / dynamic rotation.
good.hybrid: Good recovery supports dual strength/hypertrophy stress.

learn.heading: What you will learn
learn.lead: The difference between copying an elite athlete and learning from their principles — then continuing into original programmes built for modern lifters.

principles.title: Principles over cosplay
principles.body: Copying an elite athlete’s weekly template rarely transfers. Learning which principles drove adaptation — specificity, overload, recovery, and selection pressure — does.

sport.title: Sport context matters
sport.body: Bodybuilding volume, strongman event practise, and powerlifting peaking solve different problems. Filters and profiles keep those contexts distinct.

original.title: Towards original programming
original.body: Each analysis points toward The Strongest programmes that apply related principles without naming products after athletes.

1.title: Document the publicly available method
1.body: Capture what can be verified from public sources — not invented routines or private coaching notes.

2.title: Separate facts from interpretation
2.body: Historical documentation stays distinct from The Strongest’s independent analysis.

3.title: Analyse volume, intensity, specificity and recovery
3.body: Score and discuss training demands honestly, including where evidence is mixed or limited.

4.title: Build a safer modern application
4.body: Translate principles into modernised adaptations that respect recovery, technique, and individual constraints.

learn.contextBody: Elite athletes trained under different conditions — bodyweights, schedules, genetics, recovery resources, pharmacology contexts where reported historically, coaching staff, and competitive environments. A method that worked for a professional under those constraints is not a prescription for every lifter. Use these analyses to understand principles, limits, and safer modern adaptations — then choose an original programme that fits your life.

ToolsPage.label: TOOLS
ToolsPage.title: Training calculators
ToolsPage.subtitle: Useful numbers for planning — estimated 1RM, plates, DOTS, volume, attempts, and training max. Outputs are aids, not guarantees. Each tool links into the platform.
ToolsPage.calc_1rm_desc: Estimate a one-rep max from a multi-rep set using Epley — then log real singles in the app.
ToolsPage.calc_1rm_disc: Estimate only. Error grows as reps move away from a single. Never treat an e1RM as a verified PR.
ToolsPage.calc_plate_desc: Load a bar to a target weight with paired metric plates — then run the session in Today.
ToolsPage.calc_plate_disc: Assumes paired plates and the stated bar. Inventory and collar weight are not modeled.
ToolsPage.calc_dots_desc: Compute your relative strength score using DOTS or official IPF GL Points.
ToolsPage.calc_dots_disc: DOTS and IPF GL Classic — cited formulas for comparing totals across bodyweights.
ToolsPage.calc_vol_desc: Sum tonnage from load × reps × sets — then compare to the week you actually log.
ToolsPage.calc_vol_disc: Tonnage ≠ stimulus quality. Proximity to failure, exercise choice, and recovery are not in the formula.
ToolsPage.calc_attempt_desc: Sketch opener, second, and conditional third from a planning ceiling — never a guarantee.
ToolsPage.calc_attempt_disc: Sketches only — never a guarantee that any attempt will be made on the platform.
ToolsPage.calc_tm_desc: Set a programming training max (often ~90% of 1RM or e1RM) without pretending it is a tested max.
ToolsPage.calc_tm_disc: TM is a programming construct. It is not a measured max and should be revised when reality disagrees.

Tool_1RM.title: Estimated 1RM
Tool_1RM.subtitle: Estimate a one-rep max from a multi-rep set — then log real singles in the app.
Tool_1RM.body_text: Multi-rep sets can sketch a one-rep max when you need a planning number. This tool uses proven formulas (Epley, Brzycki, Lombardi, O'Conner) and limits reps to a sensible range so you aren't handed a fake precision figure. Use the estimate to set training maxes, then confirm with logged sessions.
Tool_1RM.disclaimer: Estimate only — valid for 2–12 reps. Far from a single, error grows. Never treat as a verified PR.
Tool_1RM.refuse_load: Enter a positive load in kilograms.
Tool_1RM.refuse_reps_low: Use 2 or more reps. A true single is already a 1RM — no estimate needed.
Tool_1RM.refuse_reps_high: Refuse beyond 12 reps — estimates are unreliable that far from a single.

Tool_RelativeStrength.title: Relative Strength Calculator
Tool_RelativeStrength.subtitle: Compute your relative strength score using DOTS or official IPF GL Points.
Tool_RelativeStrength.body_text: Relative strength scores only belong in the product when the formula is cited and correct. This calculator implements DOTS with OpenPowerlifting coefficients and IPF GL Points for Classic/Raw lifting. Use these to compare totals across bodyweights.
Tool_RelativeStrength.disclaimer: DOTS compares totals across bodyweights using the OpenPowerlifting curve. IPF GL is the official formula used by the International Powerlifting Federation. Federations may use different rules.
Tool_RelativeStrength.refuse_sex: Select male or female — coefficients are sex-specific.
Tool_RelativeStrength.refuse_bw: Enter a positive bodyweight in kilograms.
Tool_RelativeStrength.refuse_total: Enter a positive total (squat + bench + deadlift) in kilograms.
Tool_RelativeStrength.clamped: Bodyweight clamped to {kg} kg for the published DOTS curve.
Tool_RelativeStrength.cite_dots: DOTS (OpenPowerlifting / Tim Rohr, 2020): total × 500 / (A + B·bw + C·bw² + D·bw³ + E·bw⁴).
Tool_RelativeStrength.cite_ipf_gl: IPF GL (Classic/Raw): total × (100 / (A − B × e^(−C × bw))).
